Instructions

  1. There are 60 single-correct questions: Biology 1–15, Chemistry 16–30, Mathematics 31–45 and Physics 46–60.
  2. Each question has exactly one correct option. Correct: +4; incorrect: -1; unanswered: 0. All questions are available to attempt; there is no best-three-subject scoring rule.
  3. Use 180 minutes. An on-screen non-programmable scientific calculator is part of the 2026 examination conditions; personal calculators are not allowed under that scheme.
  4. Treat stated data and idealisations as exact unless an approximation is explicitly supplied. Log denotes base 10 and ln denotes the natural logarithm.
  5. The review PDF contains the question paper first, followed by a separate answer key and worked solutions. Keep the solutions hidden during a timed attempt.

Fixed authored order. Figures and IDs must remain linked during review.

Q1+4 / -1
An alga contains chlorophyll a and c, much fucoxanthin, and reserves consisting mainly of laminarin and mannitol. A second sample has the same brown appearance because of an added dye, but contains chlorophyll a and b and starch. Which conclusion uses the biological evidence correctly?
A) Both must be brown algae because colour determines class
B) The first fits brown algae; the dyed second sample fits green algae
C) The first fits red algae because all accessory pigments imply that class
D) The reserve products identify both as fungi regardless of chlorophyll

B) X vexillary; Y imbricate without a fixed large posterior petal
C) X imbricate; Y valvate
D) X twisted; Y vexillary

WORKED SOLUTIONS / B

Biology

Method, reasoning and common errors

Q1 Biology · medium

Diversity In the Living World / Diagnostic pigments and reserves despite an artificial colour change

Answer: (B) The first fits brown algae and the second green algae.

Why: Natural pigment complement and reserve chemistry provide linked classification characters. Fucoxanthin with chlorophyll a and c and laminarin/mannitol reserves is characteristic of brown algae. Chlorophyll a and b with starch supports green algae despite an artificial change of visible colour. A treatment that changes appearance does not automatically replace the underlying biochemical traits used for identification.

Why not the others: (A) treats an experimentally altered surface observation as decisive taxonomy. (C) ignores the specific pigment and reserve combination associated with brown algae. (D) ignores photosynthetic pigment evidence and misassigns algal reserves to a fungal diagnosis.

Key point: Classification should combine stable diagnostic characters rather than a manipulated appearance.

Q2 Biology · medium

Structural Organisation In Plants And Animals / Cyclic petal overlap versus a standard-wing-keel hierarchy

Answer: (D) X twisted and Y vexillary.

Why: X has a repeated directional overlap around the entire whorl, the defining arrangement of twisted aestivation. Y has a standard-wing-keel hierarchy: the large posterior standard overlaps the wings, which overlap the anterior keel petals. That ordered special imbricate arrangement is vexillary aestivation. The relative overlap, rather than whether the petals are fused, supplies the evidence.

Why not the others: (A) calls an overlapping whorl valvate, although valvate margins meet without overlap. (B) assigns the standard-wing-keel pattern to X even though X has uniform cyclic overlap. (C) misses the specific twisted pattern in X and denies the clear overlap in Y.

Key point: Trace who overlaps whom around the bud before naming aestivation.

Q3 Biology · hard

Cell: Structure And Functions / Pulse-chase localisation with a downstream secretory bypass

Answer: (A) ER-to-Golgi transfer is blocked.

Why: The untreated time course follows the secretory route from rough ER through Golgi to the external medium. With drug, an already synthesised stable cohort remains in the first compartment instead of appearing downstream. Normal export of a pre-existing Golgi pool shows that downstream secretion can still operate, while maintained ATP and cytosolic translation argue against a general energy or translation collapse. Together the tracer position and bypass pool localise the earliest affected transfer to ER exit or delivery towards Golgi, without identifying a particular molecular transport protein.

Why not the others: (B) contradicts preserved translation and does not explain stable accumulation of the pre-existing labelled cohort in ER. (C) predicts accumulation of the bypass pool downstream as well, contrary to its secretion. (D) would act after export and cannot explain the persistent intracellular ER localisation.

Key point: Time-resolved localisation plus a downstream bypass pool can identify a blocked trafficking stage.

Q4 Biology · medium

Plant Physiology / Transient fixation after interruption of Calvin-cycle acceptor regeneration

Answer: (C) Fixation is transiently maintained and then declines.

Why: Rubisco can use the RuBP pool already present when regeneration stops. Each fixation consumes an acceptor molecule, however, and the pool cannot sustain continued flux without its replenishing reactions. The observed order of label supports movement through a cycle whose acceptor is regenerated, rather than a single irreversible store of unlimited capacity. The treatment changes the supply of RuBP, not the identity of the initial stable C3 product.

Why not the others: (A) treats enzyme activity as sufficient despite depletion of its substrate. (B) reverses the pool balance after its production is stopped but consumption continues. (D) changes the primary fixation chemistry without a stated change in pathway.

Key point: An intact enzyme cannot sustain pathway flux when a required regenerated acceptor is exhausted.

Q5 Biology · easy

Human Physiology / Hormone replacement restores an upstream feedback signal

Answer: (B) TSH can remain near its feedback-regulated range.

Why: The feedback signal received by the hypothalamic-pituitary axis is circulating thyroid hormone. Adequate replacement can provide that signal even though the thyroid tissue no longer produces it. The missing gland prevents a normal thyroid response to TSH, but does not prevent replacement hormone from suppressing excessive upstream stimulation. Actual dosing and secretion vary, so the prediction concerns the direction of regulation rather than an exact numerical TSH.

Why not the others: (A) ignores the restored circulating feedback signal. (C) mistakes regulation of one hormone's secretion for chemical conversion into another. (D) imposes complete irreversible shutdown rather than adjustable feedback.

Key point: Feedback depends on the circulating signal, not solely on the anatomical presence of its usual source.

Q6 Biology · medium

Reproduction / Unfertilised fruit formation contrasted with asexual seed formation

Answer: (A) Parthenocarpy and apomixis.

Why: The first observation concerns development of the fruit without fertilisation, which is parthenocarpy. It need not imply embryo development or a viable seed. The second concerns asexual seed/embryo formation, the defining distinction for apomixis. Naming the developing structure prevents confusion between an ovary-derived fruit and an ovule-associated seed.

Why not the others: (D) reverses fruit formation and asexual seed formation. (B) requires multiple embryos or ordinary gametic fusion, neither of which is stated. (C) describes rejection of self-pollen rather than development of an unfertilised ovary into fruit.

Key point: Ask whether the observation is about fruit development or embryo formation.

Q7 Biology · medium

Genetics And Evolution / Ordered sibling outcomes with known carriers rather than inferred parental risk

Answer: (A) 1/4.

Given: Parents are known Aa×Aa; previous birth does not change their genotypes.

Formula/Principle: Use mutually exclusive ordered outcomes for independent births.

Step 1: For each birth, P(aa)=41​,P(Aa)=21​.

Step 2: The required outcomes are aa then Aa, or Aa then aa: P=41​21​+21​41​=41​.

Why: Carrier status is narrower than merely unaffected status. The two orders are distinct and exhaustive for the requested event. A previous affected child is consistent with the already known cross and does not impose a quota on later Mendelian outcomes.

Why not the others: (B) counts only one birth order. (C) uses all unaffected children, including AA, in place of the required carrier. (D) uses one child's carrier probability without requiring the other to be affected.

Key point: Specify both genotype classes and all admissible birth orders before multiplying.

Q8 Biology · medium

Biology In Human Welfare / Transferred antibody decay separated from vaccine-generated recall

Answer: (C) Early passive protection differs from later active memory.

Why: Transferred maternal antibodies can provide immediate protection without the infant having generated those molecules or the corresponding memory. Their decline is compatible with turnover of a finite transferred pool. A later enhanced antigen-specific response after that pool has disappeared is evidence of an acquired response established by the infant's own immune system after vaccination. The observations therefore separate the source of early effectors from the source of later recall.

Why not the others: (A) treats antibodies as self-replicating genetic templates. (B) assigns immune mechanism by age rather than by whether the recipient generated a response. (D) confuses disappearance of transferred effectors with absence of actively acquired memory.

Key point: Follow the origin and persistence of both effectors and memory when classifying immunity.

Q9 Biology · medium

Biotechnology / Target RNA without protein and a translation-site rescue

Answer: (D) Restore the binding sequence and measure both RNA and protein.

Why: Target RNA in X shows that transcription has occurred, while absent protein places the unresolved failure downstream of that observation. A change in the region needed for ribosome recruitment offers a translation-level hypothesis. Restoring that specific sequence is a causal rescue test; monitoring RNA checks that protein recovery is not merely the result of a new increase in transcription. Equal growth and identical coding sequence help narrow the interpretation without proving every alternative has vanished.

Why not the others: (A) measures a selectable marker's function, not the foreign gene's translation. (B) has no specified connection to target RNA or protein. (C) destroys transcription in the working clone and does not repair the candidate defect in X.

Key point: A selectable clone need not express the desired protein; test the stage indicated by RNA and protein evidence.

Q10 Biology · easy

Ecology / Inverted standing biomass with an upright energy flow

Answer: (B) The biomass pyramid can be inverted.

Why: Standing biomass is a stock measured at a time, whereas production and energy transfer are flows over an interval. Rapidly turning-over phytoplankton can supply consumers repeatedly while their instantaneous stock stays small. That allows the aquatic biomass pyramid to be inverted. Energy transfer still loses usable energy between trophic levels, so the energy pyramid remains upright for a consistently measured system.

Why not the others: (A) confuses organism size with trophic energy supply. (C) treats a stock as though it were a time-integrated flow. (D) ignores turnover-supported inverted biomass pyramids in aquatic systems.

Key point: Separate standing stocks from production rates before interpreting a pyramid.

Q11 Biology · medium

Genetics And Evolution / Opposite linkage phases in the two parents of an intercross

Answer: (C) 1/25.

Given: Male coupling phase and female repulsion phase have r=0.20.

Formula/Principle: Offspring aabb requires an ab gamete from each parent; identify whether that gamete is parental in each.

Step 1: In AB/ab, ab is parental, so Pm​(ab)=(1−r)/2=0.40.

Step 2: In Ab/aB, ab is recombinant, so Pf​(ab)=r/2=0.10.

Step 3: P(aabb)=0.40(0.10)=0.04=1/25.

Why: Equal recombination fractions do not give equal probabilities to every named gamete when parental phases differ. The required recessive genotype selects one particular gamete in each parent. Phase must therefore be assigned before applying multiplication across independent meioses.

Why not the others: (A) treats ab as recombinant in both parents. (B) treats it as parental in both. (D) ignores linkage and uses an unrelated single-locus recessive probability.

Key point: The same named gamete can be parental in one parent and recombinant in the other.

Q12 Biology · medium

Genetics And Evolution / Carrier-daughter pair conditional on no affected child

Answer: (A) 1/9.

Given: Per birth, carrier daughter, noncarrier daughter, unaffected son and affected son each have probability 1/4.

Formula/Principle: Condition the two-birth event on the exclusion of affected children.

Step 1: P(two carrier daughters)=(1/4)2=1/16.

Step 2: Each child is unaffected with probability 3/4, so P(neither affected)=(3/4)2=9/16.

Step 3: P=9/161/16​=1/9.

Why: The condition removes affected sons but retains two different daughter classes and unaffected sons. It does not assert that both children are girls. The numerator is already contained in the allowed event, which makes direct conditional division appropriate.

Why not the others: (B) omits the stated conditioning. (C) conditions on both children being daughters instead. (D) counts all daughter pairs rather than carrier daughters only.

Key point: Translate a family-level condition into its exact retained outcome set.

Q13 Biology · medium

Human Physiology / H-zone disappearance from explicit filament-tip geometry

Answer: (D) It shrinks from 0.4 micrometre to zero.

Given: Thin filaments extend 1.0 micrometre from each end; sarcomere length changes from 2.4 to 2.0 micrometres.

Formula/Principle: The H zone is the central thick-filament segment not overlapped by thin filaments.

Step 1: The separation of the inward thin-filament tips is H=max(0,L−2ℓthin​).

Step 2: Initially, Hi​=2.4−2(1.0)=0.4 micrometre.

Step 3: Finally, Hf​=2.0−2(1.0)=0.

Why: Sliding increases overlap without shortening either filament type. The H-zone boundary is set by the inward tips of the thin filaments, not by the thick filament's total length. In this stated symmetric geometry the tips just meet at the final length, eliminating the unoverlapped central region.

Why not the others: (A) reverses the effect of inward sliding. (B) substitutes the constant A-band length for H-zone width. (C) calculates total non-A-band length rather than the central gap between thin-filament tips.

Key point: Identify which filament boundaries define a band before using a length difference.

Q14 Biology · medium

Cell: Structure And Functions / What separate pH-rate profiles can and cannot establish

Answer: (B) Different optimal protonation environments are supported.

Why: pH affects ionisation of groups needed for active-site structure and catalysis. The separated peaks indicate different conditions for maximal measured activity. Because the substrates differ and the measurements use saturating concentrations, the plot does not provide the concentration dependence required to compare affinity. Nor does a pH profile alone distinguish reversible ionisation changes from irreversible damage after every possible exposure.

Why not the others: (A) infers molecular mass from an activity optimum without a mass measurement. (C) invents an interaction between enzymes assayed separately. (D) turns reduced rate away from an optimum into universal irreversible inactivation.

Key point: A pH-activity profile measures condition-dependent catalysis, not every molecular property of an enzyme.

Q15 Biology · hard

Ecology / Shared-species threshold for separated versus contiguous area

Answer: (C) k<64−322​.

Given: Richness doubles when area quadruples; each separate patch has 32 species.

Formula/Principle: Infer the power-law exponent and compare a set union with contiguous-area richness.

Step 1: 2=4z ⇒ z=1/2.

Step 2: For one 8A patch, S8A​=168​=322​.

Step 3: For the two-patch union, overlapping species are counted once: Sunion​=32+32−k=64−k.

Step 4: Strict superiority requires 64−k>322​ ⇒ k<64−322​≈18.75. For integer k the allowed values are 0 through 18.

Why: Doubling sampled area does not double richness when the exponent is below one. Separate patches also cannot have their species totals added without accounting for shared species. Under the explicitly assumed common habitat law, the comparison depends jointly on area scaling and overlap, not on area alone; it is not a general claim about which reserve design is always superior.

Why not the others: (A) reverses the superiority inequality. (B) compares overlap with the contiguous richness rather than subtracting it from 64. (D) excludes many positive overlaps that still meet the strict bound.

Key point: Combine species-area scaling with unique-species accounting before comparing spatial samples.

WORKED SOLUTIONS / C

Chemistry

Method, reasoning and common errors

Q16 Chemistry · medium

Chemical Bonding and Molecular Structure / Amide planarity and rotation as evidence of partial C-N multiple bonding

Answer: (C) Delocalisation gives partial C-N double-bond character.

Why: Donation of the nitrogen lone pair into the carbonyl system links the nitrogen and carbonyl orbitals. A planar arrangement supports overlap and gives the actual C-N bond more multiple-bond character than an isolated amine C-N bond. Twisting reduces that overlap, costing energy. The charged drawing is a contributor to one delocalised electronic structure, not evidence that the molecule spends alternating intervals in separately isolable forms.

Why not the others: (A) replaces a resonance hybrid by a kinetic equilibrium of drawings. (B) violates the ordinary nitrogen valence count; the contributor has an octet, not five bonds. (D) contradicts the carbonyl connectivity retained in both contributors.

Key point: Use resonance to explain measurable bond properties without treating contributors as separate molecules.

Q17 Chemistry · easy

Coordination compounds / Global charge balance and local donor counting in a bridged complex

Answer: (A) +3 and coordination number 6.

Given: Four neutral en ligands, two hydroxide ions and overall charge +4; the two metals are equivalent.

Formula/Principle: Charge balance determines oxidation state; count donor atoms attached to each metal for coordination number.

Step 1: 2x+4(0)+2(−1)=+4 ⇒ x=+3.

Step 2: Each cobalt receives four N donors from its two en ligands and two O donors from the bridges: CN=4+2=6.

Why: A bridging oxygen counts as one donor to each metal it actually contacts. Ligand count for the entire ion is therefore not the coordination number of either cobalt. Likewise a neutral chelator contributes donor atoms without contributing ionic charge.

Why not the others: (B) neglects the hydroxide charges in oxidation-state balance. (C) counts only chelate donors and omits the bridges. (D) counts the whole ion's chelate donors at one metal and assigns the wrong charge.

Key point: Count charge globally but donor contacts locally in a multinuclear complex.

Q18 Chemistry · medium

Structure of the Atom / Allowed excitation versus ground-state occupancy and unpaired spins

Answer: (D) P has two unpaired electrons, Q four, and Q is excited.

Why: P has a paired 2s orbital and two singly occupied p orbitals, giving two unpaired electrons. Q has a singly occupied 2s and three singly occupied p orbitals, giving four. Both preserve six electrons and obey Pauli exclusion, but Q promotes an electron from lower-energy 2s to 2p in this multielectron atom. The promotion costs energy even though it increases the number of unpaired electrons.

Why not the others: (A) confuses an excited state with an exclusion-rule violation. (B) assumes electron count alone fixes electronic energy. (C) reverses the occupations shown.

Key point: Check allowed occupancy separately from whether a configuration is the lowest-energy one.

Q19 Chemistry · medium

Organic Chemistry – Some Basic Principles and Techniques / Oxygen protonation followed by carbonyl-carbon activation

Answer: (B) Oxygen donates to H+ and activates the carbonyl carbon.

Why: A nucleophile supplies the electron pair used to form a new bond. Here the carbonyl oxygen is the donor and the proton is the electron-pair acceptor. Protonation increases the electron deficiency of the conjugated carbonyl system, making carbon more susceptible to a subsequent nucleophilic attack. Roles are assigned for the specific step; an atom's role in one event does not require it to be the attack site in the next.

Why not the others: (A) assigns pair donation to the wrong atom and reverses the activation effect. (C) gives a proton an electron pair it does not possess and introduces radical chemistry. (D) changes the carbon skeleton without any carbon-cleavage step.

Key point: Follow electron-pair origin and destination rather than assigning nucleophile and electrophile labels by charge alone.

Q20 Chemistry · medium

Hydrocarbons / Condition-dependent side-chain radical versus ring electrophilic chlorination

Answer: (C) X gives benzyl chloride and Y ring-chlorinated ortho/para products.

Why: Light promotes radical halogenation at the benzylic side chain, where radical stabilisation supports replacement of a methyl hydrogen. Lewis-acid-assisted chlorination instead supplies an electrophile for aromatic substitution. The pre-existing methyl group directs that ring substitution mainly to ortho and para positions. The directing group relevant to the first ring substitution is methyl, not a chlorine atom that has not yet been attached.

Why not the others: (A) reverses the stated radical and electrophilic conditions. (B) ignores the change in reaction mechanism caused by illumination and catalyst. (D) uses the wrong directing group and wrongly makes its deactivation imply meta direction.

Key point: Reaction conditions can select side-chain versus ring chemistry in the same aromatic substrate.

Q21 Chemistry · medium

Haloalkanes and haloarenes / Mixed Wurtz coupling and competing carbon-group pairings

Answer: (A) Ethane, propane and butane can form.

Why: Joining two methyl groups gives ethane, joining methyl with ethyl gives propane, and joining two ethyl groups gives butane. A mixed-halide Wurtz reaction therefore does not uniquely specify the desired cross-coupling product. The argument concerns competing carbon-group pairings, not an inability to make any propane. It also explains why symmetric alkane preparation is more straightforward with a single suitable halide.

Why not the others: (B) invents carbon removal instead of coupling. (C) excludes the cross-pairing that is explicitly allowed. (D) ignores the even-carbon products of both self-pairings.

Key point: List all allowed coupling partners before treating a mixed-halide reaction as a selective synthesis.

Q22 Chemistry · hard

Alcohols, phenols, and ethers / Two ether cleavages followed by conversion of an intermediate aliphatic alcohol

Answer: (D) Phenol, 1,2-diiodoethane and methyl iodide; 3 mol HI.

Given: Both ether links are cleaved, ordinary aliphatic OH is converted further, and aryl-O cleavage is excluded.

Formula/Principle: HI cleaves alkyl-O bonds; a generated aliphatic alcohol can consume another HI to form an iodide.

Step 1: Cleaving the phenoxyethyl bond can give Ph−O−CHX2​−CHX2​−O−CHX3​+HI​PhOH+I−CHX2​−CHX2​−O−CHX3​.

Step 2: Attack at the methyl end gives I−CHX2​−CHX2​−O−CHX3​+HI​I−CHX2​−CHX2​−OH+CHX3​I.

Step 3: Continued reaction converts the remaining alcohol: I−CHX2​−CHX2​−OH+HI​I−CHX2​−CHX2​−I+HX2​O.

Step 4: Summing consumes three HI and conserves all nine carbons among phenol, the two-carbon diiodide and methyl iodide. A different order of ether cleavages gives the same final set under the stated completion conditions.

Why: The resistant aryl-O bond leaves phenol as the aryl-containing product. Stopping after the two original ether cleavages would overlook the reactive aliphatic OH formed along the route. The explicit assumptions exclude competing elimination so that functional-group and atom accounting identify a single final set.

Why not the others: (A) breaks the excluded aryl-O bond and invents reduction to methane. (B) stops at a reactive alcohol before the stated completion. (C) replaces two C-I substitutions by reduction to ethane.

Key point: Under excess-reagent conditions, continue through reactive intermediates before counting final products and equivalents.

Q23 Chemistry · medium

Aldehydes, ketones, and carboxylic acids / An ester identified by a separated alcohol's diagnostic oxidation test

Answer: (C) Ethyl ethanoate.

Why: Among the proposed C4 esters, ethyl ethanoate releases ethanol, which is oxidised under iodoform conditions to the required methyl-carbonyl system. Methyl propanoate releases methanol, and propyl methanoate releases propan-1-ol, neither of which gives that standard positive test. Separation matters because the test is being assigned specifically to the alcohol fragment rather than to the original mixture. The molecular formula independently excludes the C3 ester.

Why not the others: (A) gives methanol rather than ethanol. (B) gives propan-1-ol, which lacks the required alcohol arrangement for a positive test. (D) has formula C3H6O2 and also gives methanol.

Key point: Use hydrolysis to map an ester's two carbon fragments before applying a diagnostic product test.

Q24 Chemistry · medium

Organic compounds containing nitrogen / Diazonium cyanation as carbon addition followed by nitrogen removal

Answer: (A) Diazotisation, cyanide substitution and nitrile hydrolysis.

Why: Diazotisation converts the amino group into a leaving diazonium group. Copper-cyanide substitution introduces a carbon-containing CN group directly on the ring, giving benzonitrile and adding one carbon to the original six. Hydrolysis converts the nitrile carbon into a carboxyl carbon and removes its nitrogen into an inorganic nitrogen-containing product. The carbon count therefore increases while the final benzoic acid contains no nitrogen.

Why not the others: (B) removes the amino substituent without introducing the extra carbon. (C) misapplies Hofmann degradation and does not place a carboxyl group on the ring. (D) only changes a halogen substituent and supplies no new carbon.

Key point: Cyanide substitution followed by hydrolysis is a carbon-adding route to an aromatic carboxylic acid.

Q25 Chemistry · medium

Solutions / Limits of formula identification from a complete-dissociation particle count

Answer: (B) Five ions form per formula unit, without unique formula determination.

Why: Under the specified complete-dissociation model, i is the ratio of solute-particle amount to analytical formula-unit amount. It therefore counts the total number of separated ions produced. Several charge-balanced stoichiometries can supply five ions, such as A2B3 with suitable 3+/2- charges or AB4 with suitable 4+/1- charges. A colligative measurement by itself does not identify ionic charges or chemical elements.

Why not the others: (A) claims uniqueness without charge or composition evidence. (C) confuses particle number with charge magnitude. (D) equates the number of particles with the number of distinct elements.

Key point: A colligative particle count can constrain stoichiometry without uniquely identifying a salt.

Q26 Chemistry · medium

Electrochemistry / Cell calibration followed by finite-dissociation equilibrium inference

Answer: (C) 8.33×10−4 M.

Given: Reference conductivity and resistance calibrate one fixed cell; acid concentration and limiting molar conductivity are supplied.

Formula/Principle: Cell constant g=κR, Λm​=1000κ/c, α=Λm​/Λm∞​, and Ka​=cα2/(1−α).

Step 1: g=0.0140(100)=1.40 cm−1,κHA​=1.40/1400=0.00100 S/cm.

Step 2: Λm​=1000(0.00100)/0.0100=100 S cm2/mol,α=100/400=0.250.

Step 3: Ka​=0.7500.0100(0.250)2​=8.33×10−4 M.

Why: Resistance depends on cell geometry, so the reference must first establish the cell constant. The molar conductivity ratio estimates the ionised fraction under the ideal model. A 25% dissociation is too large to silently replace 1-alpha by one, so the full denominator is retained.

Why not the others: (A) uses c times alpha rather than the equilibrium concentration ratio. (B) omits the undissociated-acid denominator. (D) assumes complete acid dissociation from the existence of a conductive solution.

Key point: Calibrate conductance geometry before extracting dissociation and retain a non-negligible ionisation correction.

Q27 Chemistry · hard

Chemical Kinetics / Arrhenius-ratio interpolation combined with unequal reactant concentrations

Answer: (B) 6.

Given: Both reactions are first order; two rate-constant ratios constrain their Arrhenius difference.

Formula/Principle: ln(kX​/kY​)=ln(AX​/AY​)−(EX​−EY​)/(RT) is linear in 1/T, not T.

Step 1: The reciprocal temperature at 400 K is the midpoint: 4001​=21​(3001​+6001​).

Step 2: Consequently ln(kX​/kY​)400​=21​(ln4+ln1)=ln2, so the rate-constant ratio is 2.

Step 3: Initial rates include concentration: vY​vX​​=kY​[Y]0​kX​[X]0​​=2(3)=6.

Step 4: As a consistency check, the ratio declines on warming, so the X reaction has the smaller activation energy under these assumptions.

Why: Comparing two Arrhenius equations eliminates the need to know either absolute rate constant. Interpolation must use inverse temperature because that is the linear variable. A rate-constant ratio becomes a reaction-rate ratio only after including the concentration factors and the stated first-order law.

Why not the others: (A) ignores the rate-constant difference. (C) reports the rate-constant ratio alone. (D) uses the 300 K ratio at 400 K.

Key point: Interpolate Arrhenius ratios in reciprocal temperature, then distinguish rate constants from rates.

Q28 Chemistry · medium

Thermodynamics / Equilibrium-constant algebra and the resulting standard Gibbs sign

Answer: (D) K=1/2 and the standard Gibbs change is positive.

Given: Two equilibria share A at one temperature.

Formula/Principle: Reaction addition multiplies constants; reversal inverts K and doubling squares it.

Step 1: Reverse and double the first reaction: 2B​2A,K′=1/42=1/16.

Step 2: Add A​C, cancelling one A: K=(1/16)(8)=1/2.

Step 3: ΔG∘=−RTlnK=RTln2>0.

Why: Equilibrium constants belong to specified stoichiometric equations. Changing coefficients changes the exponent pattern in the activity quotient. The standard Gibbs sign is then determined by whether the resulting dimensionless K lies above or below one; it does not specify the actual direction for every nonstandard composition.

Why not the others: (A) divides by K1 only once instead of squaring it. (B) multiplies the original constants without reversing or doubling. (C) reverses the sign in the Gibbs-constant relation.

Key point: Manipulate the reaction equation before manipulating its equilibrium constant.

Q29 Chemistry · easy

Equilibrium / Water-dominated charge balance in an extremely dilute weak acid

Answer: (A) Slightly below 7.

Why: The acid concentration is smaller than the hydrogen-ion concentration of pure water. Charge balance requires hydrogen ions to balance both hydroxide and the acid anion, so acid addition cannot make this solution alkaline. Most of this very dilute acid is ionised because Ka greatly exceeds the resulting hydrogen-ion concentration, but water remains a major source of both ions. Neglecting water or assuming a small ionised fraction is therefore inconsistent.

Given: C=10−8 M, Ka​=10−5, Kw​=10−14.

Formula/Principle: Charge balance is [H+]=[OH−]+[A−], with 0<[A−]<C.

Step 1: The bounds imply 10−7<[H+]<2C+C2+4Kw​​​≈1.052×10−7 M.

Step 2: Hence 6.978<pH<7, confirming a small acidic shift.

Why not the others: (B) ignores water and even predicts alkalinity from an acid. (C) uses the small-dissociation approximation where its predicted dissociation exceeds the total acid. (D) assumes a buffer equality that is not present.

Key point: Very dilute acid solutions require water and charge balance even when the acid is weak.

Q30 Chemistry · medium

The d- & f-block elements / Lanthanoid contraction explains a cross-period chemical resemblance without identity

Answer: (D) Lanthanoid contraction helps explain similar size and chemistry.

Why: Poor shielding by added 4f electrons across the intervening lanthanoid series increases effective nuclear attraction and contracts later atomic and ionic sizes. Hf therefore resembles Zr in size and in many +4 chemical behaviours more closely than a simple extra-shell expectation would suggest. Atomic mass is a separate property and can differ greatly even when ionic radius and common oxidation state are similar.

Why not the others: (A) treats mass as a direct valence rule. (C) contradicts the role of the intervening filled 4f series and confuses Hf chemistry with a claim about preceding atoms. (B) generalises a size/chemistry similarity to every mass-dependent or spectroscopic property.

Key point: A periodic size explanation supports related chemistry without making two elements physically identical.

Q31 Mathematics · medium

Coordinate geometry / Ellipse focal distances determine a triangle height rather than a directrix

Answer: (A) 82​.

Given: The focal separation is 6 and the sum of focal distances is 10.

Formula/Principle: Use the ellipse's distance sum and subtract squared distance equations to recover the height above the focal axis.

Step 1: The right-focus distance is 10−4=6. Write (x+3)2+y2=16,(x−3)2+y2=36.

Step 2: Subtraction gives 12x=−20, so x=−5/3. Then y2=16−(4/3)2=128/9,y=82​/3 because P is on the upper half.

Step 3: A=21​(6)(82​/3)=82​.

Worked derivation: A=3y=82​,y>0.

Why: The ellipse supplies the missing second distance, after which the difference of squares eliminates the unknown ordinate. The focal axis is a natural triangle base, but its height is y, not either focal distance. The upper-half condition removes the sign ambiguity without changing the area.

Why not the others: (B) halves the correct triangle area again. (C) treats the major-axis length as an area. (D) omits the triangle's one-half factor.

Key point: Convert focal-distance data into coordinates before using a geometric height.

Q32 Mathematics · medium

Differentiation / Flat zero crossing inside an absolute value preserves two derivatives

Answer: (D) Twice differentiable with second derivative zero.

Given: x−sinx has the sign of x for nonzero x near zero.

Formula/Principle: Resolve the absolute value and evaluate the derivative definitions at the join.

Step 1: For x positive, f=x−sinx; for x negative, f=sinx−x. Also xf(x)​→0 because sinx/x→1, so f'(0)=0.

Step 2: Away from zero, f′(x)={1−cosx,cosx−1,​x>0,x<0.​

Step 3: Using (1−cosx)/x→0, both sides of [f′(x)−f′(0)]/x tend to zero. Hence f''(0)=0.

Worked derivation: f′′(0)=x→0lim​xf′(x)​=0.

Why: An absolute value creates a corner only when its inner expression crosses zero with a sufficiently nonzero first-order slope. Here the inner expression has a flat enough contact at zero for two derivatives to survive. Its sign follows from the nonnegative derivative 1-cos x and its zero value at the origin; no power-series expansion is required.

Why not the others: (A) assumes every absolute value has a corner at an inner zero. (B) stops after the first-derivative test despite the second derivative limit existing. (C) incorrectly transfers the second derivative of another elementary function to this joined expression.

Key point: Test derivatives at the join instead of deciding smoothness from the presence of an absolute value.

Q33 Mathematics · medium

Integration / A parameter-dependent integration breakpoint and exhaustive real-solution check

Answer: (B) -1/2.

Given: The absolute-value break depends on the unknown a.

Formula/Principle: Separate parameters placing the break inside the interval from those placing it outside.

Step 1: For −1≤a≤1, I(a)=∫−1a​(a−x)dx+∫a1​(x−a)dx=1+a2.

Step 2: Setting this equal to 3/2 gives a=±1/2​, both within the assumed interval.

Step 3: For ∣a∣≥1, I(a)=2∣a∣≥2, so there are no additional roots.

Worked derivation: ∏a=(2​1​)(−2​1​)=−21​.

Why: The integration formula changes when the moving zero leaves the integration interval. Checking the outer parameter ranges proves the two inner solutions exhaust the real line. The requested product is negative because the two valid parameters have opposite signs.

Q37 Mathematics · medium

Key point: Choose a representation in which an adjacency rule is automatic before enforcing a geometric exclusion.

Q49 Physics · medium

Formula/Principle: Add the two force-per-length vectors, each of magnitude f0​=μ0​I2/(2πd).

Step 1: B attracts A to the right: fAB​=f0​(1,0).

Step 2: C repels A away from C: fAC​=f0​(−1/2,−3​/2).

Step 3: fA​=f0​(1/2,−3​/2),∣fA​∣=f0​.

Worked derivation: rB​−rC​=d(1/2,−3​/2), proving the force direction is parallel to C towards B.

Why: Reversing one current changes attraction to repulsion without changing that pair's force magnitude. The resulting vector sum is not the inward median appropriate to three equally directed currents. The geometric force directions must be assigned before using a triangle magnitude rule.

Why not the others: (A) gives the result for attraction towards both other vertices. (C) assumes equal force magnitudes imply opposite directions. (D) adds magnitudes while ignoring their different directions.

Key point: Determine current-dependent attraction or repulsion before summing parallel-wire forces geometrically.

Q57 Physics · medium

Alternating Current / A reactive secondary load reflected through an ideal transformer

Answer: (D) 4/3 A and power factor 0.6.

Given: The transformer is ideal and the reactive load has nonzero net inductive reactance.

Formula/Principle: Transform voltage and current magnitudes, while preserving real and apparent power for an ideal transformer.

Step 1: Vs​=120/3=40 V rms.

Step 2: Z=62+(10−2)2​=10 ohm,Is​=40/10=4 A.

Step 3: Ip​=Is​/3=4/3 A,cosϕ=R/Z=6/10=0.6.

Step 4: Real power is Is2​R=16(6)=96 W=120(4/3)(0.6), checking the primary result.

Worked derivation: Sp​=Ss​=160 VA,Pp​=Ps​=96 W,P/S=0.6.

Why: Ideal transformation changes voltage and current levels but does not remove the load's phase difference. Multiplying primary voltage by current gives apparent power; the reactive secondary still makes the source power factor less than one.

Why not the others: (A) uses the secondary current at the primary. (B) assumes an ideal transformer makes every load resistive. (C) reverses current scaling and uses the reactance fraction as power factor.

Key point: Carry both magnitude transformation and load phase through an ideal transformer.

Q58 Physics · hard

Ray Optics and Optical Instruments / Spherical geometry produces two strict escape-angle branches for an internal source

Answer: (A) The two radial cones, [0,θ)∪(π−θ,π].

Given: A straight internal ray reaches a spherical boundary; OP=3R/4 and the internal refractive index is 2.

Formula/Principle: Express incidence through the ray's perpendicular distance from the centre, then apply the critical-angle condition.

Step 1: The ray line's perpendicular distance from O is b=OPsinα=(3R/4)sinα.

Step 2: At the surface, the normal is a radius, so sini=b/R=(3/4)sinα.

Step 3: The critical sine is 1/2. Strict subcritical incidence requires sinα<2/3.

Step 4: On 0 through pi this means 0≤α<θorπ−θ<α≤π.

Worked derivation: i<ic​⟺(3/4)sinα<1/2⟺α∈[0,θ)∪(π−θ,π].

Why: Incidence at a curved surface is measured against the local radius, not the original OP direction. A ray initially directed inward can reach the opposite side with equally small incidence, so both near-outward and near-inward cones must be included. Critical rays are explicitly excluded; no equality endpoints are silently assigned to either behaviour.

Why not the others: (B) omits inward-directed rays escaping at the far side. (C) gives the complementary high-incidence directions. (D) ignores total internal reflection for more tangential directions.

Key point: For a curved boundary, relate the ray line's impact distance to the local surface normal before applying Snell's law.

Q59 Physics · medium

Electromagnetic Waves / Piecewise displacement-flux area gives equal magnetic fields at two different radii

Answer: (C) Equal magnetic fields with no gap conduction current.

Given: The idealised uniform electric-field region has radius a, and the gap is insulating.

Formula/Principle: B(2πr)=μ0​ε0​dΦE​/dt. The enclosed field area changes at r=a.

Step 1: For r<a, B(r)=μ0​ε0​(r/2)E˙. Thus B(a/2)=μ0​ε0​aE˙/4.

Step 2: For r>a, the enclosed flux uses area pi a squared: B(r)=μ0​ε0​2ra2​E˙. Thus B(2a)=μ0​ε0​aE˙/4.

Step 3: The values are equal even though one branch rises with r and the other falls as 1/r.

Worked derivation: B(a/2)/B(2a)=1,Iconduction,gap​=0.

Why: A changing electric flux contributes to magnetic circulation without transporting charge through the dielectric gap. Inside the plate radius only part of that flux is enclosed; outside, its entire value is enclosed while the loop circumference keeps growing. Applying one radial formula on both sides would give the wrong ratio.

Why not the others: (A) misuses the outer branch inside and invents conduction through the gap. (B) extends the inner branch outside and denies the changing-flux term. (D) omits displacement current from Maxwell's law.

Key point: Use the correct enclosed electric-flux area on either side of a charging capacitor's plate radius.

Q60 Physics · easy

Nuclei / Efficiency change masks activity decay while background stays fixed

Answer: (B) 100 counts/min.

Given: Initial source-only signal is 80 counts/min and background is 20 counts/min; efficiency doubles after one half-life.

Formula/Principle: Detected source signal is proportional to efficiency times activity; background is added separately.

Step 1: Decay alone halves source activity, so at unchanged efficiency the signal would be 80/2=40 counts/min.

Step 2: Doubling efficiency gives Sf​=2(40)=80 counts/min.

Step 3: Cf​=Sf​+20=100 counts/min.

Worked derivation: Cf​=2(80⋅2−1)+20=100 counts/min.

Why: The detector can report the same mean rate even though half the radioactive nuclei have decayed. Instrument efficiency changes the fraction of emissions recorded, while the background is specified as unchanged. These are expected rates, not a claim that random observed counts are identical in every minute.

Why not the others: (A) accounts for decay but ignores the efficiency change. (C) doubles the original source signal without decay. (D) halves the total including a background that does not decay.

Key point: Separate activity, detection efficiency and background before interpreting a count-rate change.
